Ändra text eller datum här; ta bort en rad för att stryka ett inlägg. Godkänd av grundaren 2026-10-24; de fem första postas samma kväll med 40 minuters mellanrum. Från 2026-10-25 ett per dag kl. 18 (Viktor 2026-10-24). 2026-11-08: Viktor tog bort inlägg vars bild hade svensk text för att ompublicera dem med den engelska bilden ("stor ökning" med engelsk bild); de gamla raderna har "removed", de nya "repost": true. "credit" postas som svar direkt under inlägget.

items.text: Inside Vitki, an open tool for Sweden's runic inscriptions: pattern maps of all 2,321 Viking-age runestones, statistics in R, what the evidence says about each stone, and the research gaps. Free and open source (Swedish interface): vitkirunor.se

Screenshot of Vitki's statistics page (Swedish interface): a grid of questions computed in R about carvers, dating, regions and language, with a summary of what the statistics say together.
Screenshot of Vitki's stone overview (Swedish interface): how well the methods support the carver given in the runic database, with counts of stones and suggestions for interpretation.
Screenshot of Vitki's research gaps page (Swedish interface): key figures for the 2,321 Viking-age runestones at the top, and cards for open questions where the app's analyses can add to research.

items.text: What a 3D scan shows that the eye can't: runestone Sö 113 in Vitki. Raking light, depth below the surface, the V-angle of each cross-section and 254 groove profiles. Scan: L. Kitzler Åhfeldt, Swedish National Heritage Board, CC BY 4.0 (credit in alt text).

images.alt: The runestone Sö 113 in four digital raking-light renderings from a 3D scan, lit at 20 degrees from north-west, north-east, south-east and south-west; the runes show differently depending on the light. Scan by Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt, Swedish National Heritage Board, research project Runristandets dynamik, CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.11951255.

Depth map of Sö 113: depth below the stone surface in millimetres, from pale yellow (level with the surface) to black (about 5 mm deep). The rune bands and runes stand out as dark lines; scale bar 100 mm. Scan by Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt, Swedish National Heritage Board, research project Runristandets dynamik, CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.11951255.

Sö 113 in grey relief with every measured cross-section of the grooves marked as a coloured dot by its V-angle, from about 70 to 150 degrees; letters A to L mark individual cross-sections. Scan by Laila Kitzler Åhfeldt, Swedish National Heritage Board, research project Runristandets dynamik, CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.11951255.

Chart of 254 groove profiles from the runes of Sö 113: height above the groove bottom (mm) against distance from the bottom (mm), thin grey lines with the median profile in red, a V-shaped groove about 3 mm deep. items.text: Hello Bluesky! Vitki is an open research platform for Sweden's runic inscriptions: statistics on every runestone, 3D analysis of carved grooves, and a model that suggests lost runes. Open data, open code. Here we share what the stones show.

Hávamál was composed about a thousand years ago and reached us in a single manuscript. We read it as it asks to be read: as advice to a person. On arriving as a guest, on friendship, sleepless nights – and what is left of a life.

items.text: Two in three Swedish runestones have no carver named in the runic database. In a blind test on 769 stones with the answer hidden, Vitki's suggestions were right four times in five. Here are the five strongest candidates – and how they are worked out.

Around 1035 more than one runestone in three asked God to help the dead person's soul. Fifty years later only one in ten did – though the cross was still carved on the stones. Where did the prayer go?

14 Swedish runestones were raised for a daughter, against 268 for a son. But where daughters appear, they appear in their own way: the stones are late, and in Uppland more than one in three is a bridge.

Seven scholars have given the Malt stone seven different meanings. We let a model that has learnt the runic language from thousands of inscriptions read it instead. It confirms the core, chooses between disputed runes – and shows why a full text is out of reach.

items.text: Curses, Thor and lead amulets against fever. We went through all 6,753 runic inscriptions in the Scandinavian Runic-text Database looking for magic: in the Viking Age people protected the stone in the south and the soul in the north.

Runes were carved in wood, bone and metal, but stone is what survived. Did the carvers know it would? Thirty-two Viking-age stones say so themselves. And us: what of what we write today will be left in a thousand years?

Only six of 2,321 Swedish runestones name Thor or carry his hammer. They were carved among Christian stones, and several mimic the shape of the cross. Did Thor come to the runestones as an answer to the cross?
Fifty-nine runestones in Skåne, and not one names a king or a realm. Where did people belong in Skåne when the stones were raised, between Denmark and what would become Sweden?

items.text: Women help raise one runestone in four, but only one in thirty is raised for a woman. Were women the vanguard of Christianity, as is often said? Our figures point to inheritance instead.

Around Enköping, æftiᛦ is written with an ordinary r five times as often as in the rest of Sweden. Was it the local pronunciation? The trail leads to one carver, Erik, and to those who carved after him.

items.text: 112 Viking-age runic inscriptions have never been interpreted beyond a single word. We tried them with the codebreakers' tools – al-Kindi's frequency analysis and Friedman's index of coincidence – and with a language test of our own.

One in five names on Swedish runestones is still borne today, and names with a god in them survived best. But power changed its words: the jarl became a duke, Svitjod became Sverige, and drengr, the hero, a farmhand.

Hávamál was composed about a thousand years ago and reached us in a single manuscript. We read it as it asks to be read: as advice to a person. On arriving as a guest, on friendship, sleepless nights – and what is left of a life.

A way of reading the world that began with nature: thunder driving across the sky, trees that people were made from, horses that drew day and night. A personal article – and about what we cannot follow.

items.text: More than one runestone in three has no style group in the runic database, and the gaps are not random. Damaged, uninterpreted and peripheral stones vanish from the dating most often – and they don't behave like the rest.
Västergötland raised its runestones with its own hands; Uppland had others do the work. We counted the commonest words on the runestones province by province – and the words stayed at home.
The word stav means at least six things when it comes to runes. Five runestones mention staffs raised beside the stone. None survives, but the statistics show where they stood.
Fifty-nine runestones in Skåne, and not one names a king or a realm. Where did people belong in Skåne when the stones were raised, between Denmark and what would become Sweden?

Around 1035 more than one runestone in four ended with a prayer. Fifty years later more ended with the carver's own name. But the signature didn't follow demand – it followed the carvers, from master to apprentice.
Raising runestones came from the Danish realm and took root first in Götaland – and Västergötland wrote most like the Danes. At the border there is a silent belt where almost no stones were raised.

No one on Sweden's runestones was called Freja. Today 7,000 Swedes are. We counted every Old Norse first name in use now: the stones' names are ageing with their bearers, while the gods' names (Freja, Idun, Embla, Loke) grow.

Many runestones have places where runes have been lost. We are building a model that suggests what stood there and how sure it is. Here is how it is tested: six trials with known answers and calibrated percentages.

Seven scholars have given the Malt stone seven meanings. We let a model trained on thousands of runic inscriptions read it instead. It confirms the core, chooses between disputed runes – and shows why a full text is out of reach.
A personal piece by Vitki's founder Viktor Kvant: a book in the family magazine rack, the raven above the treetops, and why Vitki came to be – with three stanzas of Hávamál.

New in the series The old lands: Skåne around AD 1000, a Danish land in change. Uppåkra fades, the king builds ring forts and a church in Lund. From the shore at Trelleborg to the land assembly east of Lund.
Denmark had been Christian since Harald Bluetooth, yet Danish runestones almost never prayed for the dead. Two of the five that do before 1050 stand six kilometres apart near Randers.

Where the editors wrote three dots, they chose not to guess. Two models check each other: one proposes the word in the gap, the other tests whether the text is language at all – and the edition has the last word. Part II of Interpret, he who can.

Around Enköping, æftiᛦ is written with an ordinary r five times as often as in the rest of Sweden. Was it the local pronunciation? The trail leads to one carver, Erik, and to those who carved after him.

Miklagarðr, Serkland, Orkney, Greenland: we counted every place outside Scandinavia on runestones and in sagas. Swedish stones look east, sagas about the Icelanders' ancestors west – and sagas about the ancient past east again.

We laid the soil map over every runestone still in place. The stones stand not on the clay but at its edge, on dry ground near the grave fields. And half of the Mälaren valley's lead is explained by neither soil, settlement nor water.

Can a 3D scan help read a damaged runestone? With scan traces our language model got 60% of hidden words right instead of 54%. But the pairing of scan and text saw the answer, so the real gain is unproven.

items.text: Who died in the east and the west? On Swedish runestones, sons and brothers died abroad three to four times as often as fathers and husbands – and mothers and siblings raised the stones. The journeys belonged to the young.

How good is our runic text model, really? A day behind the scenes: five processes computing, a reading of the Rök stone that fails honestly, a comparison with DeepMind's Ithaca, and the sources we plan to feed the model next.

Four stones for two children. Testing names against chance, we linked 42 families across 95 runestones. Nine in ten links are already in the runologists' list. Of three new ones, one is probably wrong.

Research report: a woman is among the raisers on 31 % of Swedish runestones in Svealand, 17 % in Götaland. Pre-registered, with age, region and carver held constant, and in both halves of the material.
Research report: sons and brothers died abroad on 10 % of their runestones, fathers and husbands on 3 %. Pre-registered and robust to every check. The journeys east and west belonged to the young.
Research report: runestones gather in family groups. Stones within 500 m name the same person eight times as often as stones 2–10 km apart, and groups stand by grave fields in four cases of five.

Gerlög outlived her daughter Inga and inherited from her – cut into the rock at Hillersjö. The old lands: Attundaland around AD 1000, where great men wrote in stone that they had made the assembly place.

Research report: in western Uppland ʀ was written with the ordinary r-rune five times as often as elsewhere in Sweden, around Holm in Vittinge, where the carver Erik never wavered. A writing tradition?
Research report: stin for stain has been used to date the monophthong in Sweden. On the runestones it grows rarer, from 69 to 22 %. The late Upplandic spelling looks like a written norm, not speech.

New research report: a model groups runestones that may share a carver – also where no named carver fits. In a locked final test, 42 % of the runologists' own same-hand pairs landed in the same group, against 7 % for neighbouring stones.

Methods report v4: in a locked blind test, carver suggestions from runic texts matched Rundata's carver on 82 % of the confident ones (nearest stone: 44 %). Against runologists' same-hand groups: no better than neighbours.

Only one Swedish runestone in sixteen says how the dead died: battle, betrayal, a sinking ship, a mother of small children, men in white christening robes. After 1050 the stones tell of death half as often.

Research report: half of Swedish runestones turn their inscription within 45 degrees of the road, against a quarter by chance. Not towards the sun, not towards the farm. The carvers wrote for those passing by.

Research report: on Swedish runestones parent and child share a name element, like Holmger and Holmfast, in 5.3 % of pairs, against 2.8 % by chance. A custom for some families, alive through the whole runestone era.

Research report: ordered only by language and content, Uppland's runestones fall in the same sequence as the stylistic chronology built on their ornament. Two independent clocks, showing roughly the same time.
In Fjädrundaland, western Uppland, one runestone in three bears a cross, against six in ten in the rest of Uppland. Balle's stone for Brune, who "died in christening robes", has none either.

Research report: Viking-age runestones were raised by the water of their own time. 64 % stand within 500 m of the shore of AD 1050, against 46 % of the land around them. Grave fields draw more strongly. Holds in all checks.

New series, The old lands. In the Viking Age Södertörn was an island, Tören. Its outer half around AD 1000: farms in forest clearings, a grave field by every village, hillforts on the heights, an assembly site by the sea.

New research report: a discovery engine that searches one half of the runestones for unexpected associations, freezes the list and tests it on the other half. Of 28 associations found in the first half, 14 held in the second.

Were Uppland's old folklands real borders in the Viking Age? Of 999 random divisions of the same hundreds, only 2 separate the runestones as much as the folklands do. One border we had to give up on the way: at vs æftiR.

Seven runestones, all in Uppland, say the dead man died 'in white clothes' – in his baptismal robes, newly baptised. On four of the five where the raisers can be read, a woman is among them: his mother or his wife.

Why does Viking-age Norway have only 66 runestones, and Sweden more than 2,300? Norwegians almost never wrote that they had a stone raised; around Lake Mälaren professional carvers worked for patrons. And the Norwegian stones remember women more often.

Why do runes look the way they do? Straight strokes, almost no horizontals – and around 700 the row shrank from 24 to 16 signs. Across all Swedish runestones the k-rune stands for g one time in six, b for p one in four.

I grew up at Ättekulla in Helsingborg, where burial mounds lay at the edge of the forest. Who lay in them? Bronze Age families, for almost a thousand years – the mounds were already ancient when the Vikings raised their runestones. Most are gone now.

25 Swedish runestones remember one journey: Ingvarr's expedition to Serkland. We took them out, under a plan locked in advance. About half of the stones' eastward lead vanished – yet they still look east more than the Icelanders' sagas.
Odensvi, Torsåker, Ullvi: the old gods live on in Swedish place names. Cult-place names are thickest around Lake Mälaren, and hardly any parish with one lacks an Iron Age grave field.

New in the series The old lands: Gotland around AD 1000. A land of its own in the sea: farms that moved about their land, harbours along the whole coast, more silver in the ground than anywhere else, one assembly for the island.

Could Viking-age people read the runestones? One in three Swedish runestones points at itself – 'this stone' – and one in nine names its carver. But only ten of 2,321 ask outright for a reader: interpret, he who can.

New research report: runestones without a carver grouped by how they are written. Tested on known carvers, a group is on average 86 % the same carver, against 71 % for nearby stones – but that the unsigned groups are one hand is not shown.

Merry Christmas from Vitki! The word jól occurs 81 times in Heimskringla: feasts, gifts, killings and a king who moved Yule to the Christian date. On the runestones: not once. And Júli on Sö 362? Named after a hedgehog.

New in the series The old lands: Värend, the largest of Småland's small lands. A lake country ringed by forest around AD 1000: large villages, a great mound at Ingelstad and perhaps an assembly by Helgasjön.

On a grave slab in Skänninge, Åsa is called both daughter and maiden. The rare runic word for maiden appears on just 4 of 2,320 Swedish runestones – and it seems to have meant an unmarried woman, not a young girl.

New research report: an open model links runestones that share names, tested against chance at the same distance. It recovers 40 % of the stones runologists have tied together in families, and 92 % of its 61 links stand in their list.
Sweden has 1,304 Iron Age hillforts; only 73 are listed as excavated. 64% lie within 500 m of the water, against 48% of the hills around them. In the legends they became homes of giants.

New in the series The old lands: Möre, the coast by the Kalmar Sound around AD 1000. Fertile clay between forest and sea, villages by the rivers, ships offshore – a land judged by Östergötland's law, not by that of Småland's Tiohärad.
We read Fornvännen from its first volume in 1906. Part I: the founders – von Friesen, Brate, Lindqvist, Wessén, Jansson – who mended stones, hunted lost ones in church walls and asked our questions.
A runestone became a baking slab for soldiers and cracked in the rain. Another lay as a bridge for 200 years, a third was cut into a millstone. The stones' second lives, from the old editions.

Along the river Lagan in Finnveden almost every grave was a mound. At Fallnaveka two people were buried with two horses, two dogs, two pigs, sheep and goat. The old lands: western Småland around AD 1000.
From 1970 runologists began to count – and to argue about how. Part II: a Varangian's name in Hagia Sophia, a generous quarrel over statistics, Futhark as a journal, and the Rök stone read anew.

Did the Viking Age end in 1066? In Sweden runestones went on for decades: nearly a third of those with a firm style group are later. Around 1100 the runes moved into the churches and onto grave slabs.

Viking-age carvers had 16 runes for some 30 sounds, so some added a dot: i became e. In Götaland dotted runes go with crosses. In Uppland dots stayed rare, while the ós-rune spread on the late stones.

Can you count your way to the Vikings? One runestone cannot tell you whether it is unusual; all 2,321 together can. How Vitki locks its questions before counting, and says where the numbers fall short.

Who held the chisel? 3 in 4 Swedish runestones have no known carver. Vitki learns carvers' traits from signed stones only, right first on 71 % of them – but a hand with no name still lands in a known workshop.

How do you measure how a runestone's runes were cut, and not the serpent around them? A step-by-step guide to Vitki's groove analysis on M 15 at Skön, Medelpad: face the carved side, check the bands, count with the rune as the unit.

Which runestones have scholars written about? Part III: just over half of Sweden's runestones are never mentioned by number in the journals. Not province or period decides, but how long the text is and whether the stone survives.

Where did the elves go? We read all 64 elves in Old Norse literature. In the Edda they stand beside the gods, in the sagas never – and in Sweden they are all but absent from place names and runestones. Old Norse beings, part 2.

Many runestones were carved by the same unknown hand. A model now points out such groups – and in a locked test it put the runologists' own same-hand pairs together six times as often as neighbouring stones.
The giants of Old Norse literature: named jötnar in the Edda, trolls in the sagas – and in Swedish place names they cling to the oldest graves. Old Norse beings, part 3.
375 of 2,321 Swedish runestones carry a bear name – Bjôrn, Þorbjôrn, Ásbjôrn – twice as many as the wolf names. In the sagas the bear is a rare word. Old Norse beings, part 4.

In saga prose the word dreki means a ship in 78 per cent of cases. In the Eddic poems the dragon is ormr. On the runestones the serpent winds round the text on three stones in four – but is never named. Old Norse beings, part 5.

How do you count a rune animal? Two independent readers, a fixed codebook – and every kind of picture tested against another. The 17th- and 18th-century drawings held for the animal's main features; the depth images from 3D scans did not.
Some thirty clay moulds for small silver women lie in Birka's black earth – the 'valkyries'. We followed norns, dísir, valkyries and fylgjur through the Edda and the sagas. Old Norse beings, part 6.
In the sagas the wolf is hardly ever an animal. Half of the time it is a human being – usually an enemy seen in a dream. Old Norse beings, part 7.

At Fróðá in Iceland the dead sat by the fire every evening, until the living took them to court. In Old Norse literature the dead come home almost only in the sagas of Icelanders. Old Norse beings, part 8.
